newsitem.title: ISRAEL: U.S. tries again to save Mideast peace.
newsitem.headline: U.S. tries again to save Mideast peace.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton is working on a package to prevent already fraying Middle East peace from completely unravelling, Israeli and U.S. sources say.
But neither Israelis nor Palestinians expect his meeting with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu next Monday can stitch up relations with Palestinian President Yassser Arafat.

"They are not going to come out of the White House with anything that will move the process forward," a Western official, who spoke on condition he not be identified, said on Thursday. "It's going to take more than one quick bilateral meeting to repair the damage done to this peace process."

Netanyahu's decision to build a Jewish settlement on the edge of Arab East Jerusalem has tugged at the threads of trust and security cooperation that Washington helped weave into the fabric of Israeli-PLO peace agreements.
"Everything between us and the Israelis is frozen both on the political and security levels," Arafat's spokesman Nabil Abu Rdainah said.

The deadlock has heightened fears in Western and Arab capitals that sporadic violence since the groundbreaking for the settlement last month could escalate into the kind of gunbattles seen last September between Israeli and Palestinian security forces that almost killed the whole process.

Israeli and U.S. sources said Washington had not settled on a final package of measures. They said brokering a resumption of Israeli-Palestinian talks would probably require another shuttle to the region by U.S. peace coordinator Dennis Ross followed by an inaugural visit of Secretary of State Madeleine Albright.
Among measures the United States is weighing is an Israeli proposal to speed up talks on a permanent settlement of the conflict between two peoples over one land.

The so-called "final status talks", which have not resumed since Netanyahu took office, are scheduled under the Oslo peace accords to be completed by May 4, 1999. But Israel wants them finished by the end of this year in the hope of putting pressure on Arafat and getting a better deal. Arafat could be induced into gambling on such go-for-broke talks by Israeli concessions, Western diplomats said.

Israel would undertake to freeze new Jewish settlements on occupied Arab land and would ease restrictions on the daily lives of Palestinians, the sources said. In return it would insist Arafat again crack down on Islamic militants who have resumed suicide attacks against Israelis.
"This is not just an Israeli demand. There will be no U.S. initiatives until Arafat is seen to be acting against terrorism," the Western official said.

Some Israeli media have speculated that Netanyahu would also propose to Clinton a six-month suspension of work on the controversial settlement on a hill between Jerusalem and Bethlehem, known as Jabal Abu Ghneim or Har Homa.

But Israeli officials have ruled out such a concession which could lose Netanyahu the nationalist and settler wing of his coalition, driving the Likud party leader into a grand coalition with Shimon Peres's opposition Labour party.
"There's no basis whatsoever to this," Netanyahu's aide David Bar-Illan said of a Har Homa deal. "This is not a matter for negotiations and it will not be on the bargaining table," he told Reuters.

"Netanyahu is talking tough on Har Homa and will talk tough again in Washington when he meets AIPAC," said an Israeli official, referring to the lobby group, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee.
"He can afford to do so because he knows it won't even be on the agenda. He knows Clinton won't ask him to backtrack," the official said.

It is not clear, however, whether Arafat will accept an American compromise which leaves out Har Homa. The settlement has become a symbol in the battle for Jerusalem, one of the issues on the "final status" table.

"It is not possible to put the peace process back on track while settlement activity, land confiscations and steps that pre-empt final status negotiations continue," Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat told Reuters.
After meeting Jordan's King Hussein this week Clinton said that to put peace back on track he was "personally prepared to do anything I can."
Israeli and Palestinian officials were sceptical, however, of U.S. reports that Clinton would convene marathon talks of the kind that led to Israeli-Egyptian peace at Camp David.
